opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the kind of questions I care about right now, and what kind of environment actually lets you pursue them seriously.

For the past several years, a lot of my work has been about visual representation learning: how models see, how they build an understanding of the world. More and more, I've come to believe that the current paradigm, which is heavily centered on language, is not the full picture. Language is an incredibly powerful interface, but it's a compressed, human-made abstraction. If we really want systems that understand the physical world, that can reason about space, about cause and effect, about how things move and interact, then I think vision and world modeling have to sit at the core. That's a bet, and it's a bet that's somewhat against the mainstream.

When you're making that kind of bet, the setting matters a lot. In academia you have freedom, which I value enormously, and you have wonderful students. But frontier exploration today also requires serious compute, serious engineering, and a team that can iterate quickly at scale. Academia struggles to provide that. On the other hand, in a big company you have resources, but you're usually part of a larger roadmap. The priorities are set by product needs or by whatever the dominant direction is. It's very hard to say, "I want to spend the next few years pushing in a direction that may look unfashionable right now."

A startup sits in between in an interesting way. You can define the research agenda from first principles. You can build a culture that is research-first but also very serious about execution. And you can gather people who share the same conviction, which I think is underrated. When everyone on the team believes the problem is important and the direction is right, you move very differently than when people are just following a plan handed down to them.

Of course, it's risky. A startup forces you to be honest. You can't hide behind papers, and you can't hide behind a big organization. Either the ideas work or they don't. But I actually see that as a strength. Some of the most important progress in this field has come from small, focused groups willing to take a non-consensus view and stick with it long enough to find out whether it's true.

So for me, it's less about wanting to be an entrepreneur for its own sake, and more that this felt like the most honest way to chase the problem I think matters most right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a startup lets him define the research agenda from first principles and presents it as the right setting for pursuing his frontier questions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that frontier exploration today needs a few things at once, and it's become very hard to find them all in one place.

In academia, I had freedom. I could pick any problem I found interesting, I could be wrong for a long time, and nobody would stop me. That's genuinely precious, and I don't want to downplay it. But the frontier has moved to a scale where ideas alone aren't enough. You need compute, you need engineering depth, you need data infrastructure, and you need people who can stay on one problem for years rather than for one paper cycle. A university lab, however good, is structurally built around students graduating and around publishing, not around sustained building.

In a large company, you have the opposite problem. The resources are there, but the direction is set by the business. If you want to go somewhere the product roadmap doesn't point, you're always negotiating. And the big labs have, understandably, converged on a fairly narrow path. Everyone is scaling roughly the same recipe. That's rational for them, but it means the space of unexplored directions is actually growing, not shrinking, because fewer people are willing to leave the main road.

So a startup, for me, is about owning the question. I get to decide what the problem is, and I get to build the team and the infrastructure around that question rather than fitting the question to someone else's infrastructure. It's also a forcing function. In research it's easy to stay in the comfortable zone where something looks promising on a benchmark. When you're building something that has to work end to end, reality pushes back very quickly, and I find that pressure clarifying. It tells you which ideas were real.

I'd add one more thing. I think some of the most important work in the next few years won't come from one more percent on the standard recipe. It will come from people asking different questions about representation, about how models understand the world, about what we're actually optimizing for. Those are long-horizon bets. A startup is one of the few places where you can make a long-horizon bet and still have the resources to actually test it, as long as you're disciplined about it. That combination is what I was looking for, and I couldn't find it anywhere else.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a startup lets them “own the question” and decide what problem to pursue, directly linking self-defined research problems to having a startup.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal is being able to connect a research question directly to what we build. You can choose a direction, put a small team around it, and learn quickly from whether the idea actually works. That makes a startup an attractive setting for exploration.

There’s a tension, of course. You need enough focus to make progress as a company, but enough freedom to pursue something whose value isn’t obvious yet. I think the key is to make those two things reinforce each other: the research opens up new possibilities for the product, and building the product exposes gaps in the research. That’s the kind of environment I’d want to create.

r001.rationale: The response says a startup lets you choose a direction, but does not clearly say that defining the research problems yourself may require having your own startup.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the appeal is the freedom to connect a research question to something we can actually build. In frontier research, you often don’t know the right direction at the beginning. You need room to experiment, learn from failures, and change your assumptions. A startup can give a small team the ability to move through that cycle quickly.

Of course, you have constraints—compute, funding, time. But those constraints also force you to be clear about what you believe. What is the experiment that really matters? Where can you make a contribution beyond simply doing more of what already works? That combination of scientific freedom and responsibility is what makes starting a company compelling to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes a startup as giving freedom to experiment and choose important experiments, but does not clearly say that defining the research problems oneself may require having one’s own startup.
